title: The One Minute Manager
author: Ken Blanchard and Spencer Johnson
theme: Good management comes from a few short, simple habits that make people clear about goals and honest feedback part of everyday work.
summary: Ken Blanchard and Spencer Johnson tell their message as a short parable. A young man searches for an effective manager. He meets bosses who care only about results, whose teams suffer, and bosses who care only about people, whose organisations struggle. Finally he finds a manager who gets strong results and also has loyal, motivated staff. This manager says his methods take very little time, so he calls himself the One Minute Manager. The young man interviews him and his team to learn three simple practices.

The first is setting one minute goals. Manager and employee agree on a small number of goals, describe what good performance looks like, and write each goal briefly on a single page. Because the goals are short, the employee can reread them often and check whether current behaviour matches them. Most confusion at work, the book suggests, comes from people not knowing what is expected of them.

The second is giving one minute praisings. Instead of waiting to catch people making mistakes, the manager looks for them doing something right. Praise is given soon after the event, is specific about what went well, and says how it helps the organisation. With new staff, the manager praises progress that is only roughly right and builds from there.

The third is the one minute reprimand. When an experienced person makes a mistake, the manager responds promptly and says clearly what went wrong and how he feels about it. He then makes clear that he still values the person. The criticism is aimed at the behaviour, never at the individual's worth.
Underneath these habits is a simple belief: people who feel good about themselves tend to produce good results. The book argues that a little time invested in people pays back many times over.
takeaway: Agree on clear written goals, catch people doing things right, and correct mistakes quickly while respecting the person.

questions.q: In what form do the authors present their ideas?
options: A statistical study of large firms
A short story about a young man seeking an effective manager
A collection of interviews with CEOs
A technical manual on performance appraisal
questions.why: The book is a parable following a young man who searches for, and learns from, an effective manager.

questions.q: What was wrong with the managers the young man met before the One Minute Manager?
options: They focused on either results or people, but not both
They spent too little time in meetings
They had no formal training
They worked only in small companies
questions.why: Some cared only about results and others only about people, and each approach had clear costs.

questions.q: Why are one minute goals kept brief and written on a single page?
options: To satisfy legal requirements
To reduce printing costs
So they can be reread quickly and compared with current behaviour
So the manager does not need to discuss them
questions.why: Short written goals let people check often whether what they are doing matches what is expected.

questions.q: According to the book, a major cause of poor performance is that people:
options: Are paid too little
Dislike their colleagues
Have too much free time
Do not clearly know what is expected of them
questions.why: Clear goals are the first practice because unclear expectations lead to confusion and weak results.

questions.q: What attitude underlies the one minute praising?
options: Catching people doing something right
Praising everyone equally at year end
Avoiding feedback to keep the peace
Rewarding only senior staff
questions.why: The manager actively looks for good work to recognise rather than waiting for errors.

questions.q: How should a one minute praising be delivered?
options: In writing several months later
Only during formal reviews
Soon after the event and specific about what went well
In general terms so no one feels singled out
questions.why: Prompt, specific praise tells people exactly which behaviour to repeat.

questions.q: How does the manager handle a new employee who is still learning?
options: Waits until the work is perfect before giving any praise
Praises progress that is roughly right and builds on it
Reprimands every small error
Leaves the person to learn alone
questions.why: Recognising approximately right behaviour encourages learners to keep improving step by step.

questions.q: In a one minute reprimand, what does the manager do after stating the mistake?
options: Assigns the task to someone else
Records it for the annual review
Asks the team to vote on a penalty
Reaffirms that he still values the person
questions.why: The reprimand ends by making clear that the person is respected even though the behaviour was not acceptable.

questions.q: What is the target of criticism in a one minute reprimand?
options: The person's specific behaviour
The person's character
The whole team
The company's policies
questions.why: Criticism addresses what was done, not the individual's worth.

questions.q: Which belief sits underneath all three practices?
options: Fear is the best motivator
Managers should avoid close contact with staff
People who feel good about themselves tend to produce good results
Goals should be kept secret to avoid pressure
questions.why: The book argues that building people's confidence and clarity is what drives strong performance.
